finding.claim: The /fetch handler passes an unvalidated, attacker-supplied query parameter directly to http.Get, and echoes the upstream response body back to the caller, giving a non-blind SSRF.
finding.source: r.URL.Query().Get("target") at main.go:15 (HTTP query parameter, attacker-controlled)
finding.sink: http.Get(target) at main.go:16 (server-side HTTP fetch), response streamed via io.Copy(w, resp.Body) at main.go:22

trace.note: /fetch is registered to the fetch handler with no auth or middleware
target read from the query string with no transformation
raw string passed to http.Get, which follows redirects by default
upstream response body copied back to the requester, making the SSRF non-blind

finding.guards_checked: None on this path: no scheme check, no host allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local IP block, no port restriction, no redirect limit or CheckRedirect, no response size limit. Go http.Get only speaks http/https, so file:/gopher: are not reachable through this sink. Reachable targets include loopback services, RFC 1918 hosts, and cloud metadata (169.254.169.254).

verdict.reason: main.go:41 routes /fetch to fetch, which reads the unvalidated `target` query parameter at main.go:15, passes it straight to http.Get at main.go:16, and copies the response body back to the caller at main.go:22 with no scheme, host, or IP check. The allowlist at main.go:9-12 and the check at main.go:27 only protect the separate /safe handler (main.go:42), not /fetch.

finding.claim: The /safe handler's host allowlist is applied only to the initial URL. The default client follows redirects to any destination, so an allowed host that redirects to an internal address bypasses the allowlist. Exploitability depends on the allowed hosts redirecting, which the code alone does not show.
finding.source: r.URL.Query().Get("target") at main.go:26 (HTTP query parameter, attacker-controlled)
finding.sink: http.Get(u.String()) at main.go:31, with the response body returned at main.go:37

finding.guards_checked: Exact-match host allowlist on u.Hostname() at main.go:27, fail-closed: userinfo tricks (http://images.example.org@evil.com/) and fragment tricks (http://evil.com#@images.example.org/) resolve to the real host and are rejected; trailing-dot and case variants are rejected. The validator and fetcher use the same Go parser and object, so there is no parser differential. Scheme is not checked, but Go's client rejects non-http(s) schemes. Not guarded: redirect targets (no CheckRedirect), resolved IP addresses (the allowlist covers names only). Bypass needs an allowed host that redirects to an internal destination, either attacker-controlled or with an open redirect; not shown in this code.

verdict.guard_found: Exact-match hostname allowlist on the parsed hostname: `allowed[u.Hostname()]` at main.go:27, which fails closed (403) before the fetch at main.go:31. The rest of the trace is accurate: /safe is registered at main.go:42, url.Parse is at main.go:26, the fetch is at main.go:31, and the body is copied back at main.go:37.
verdict.reason: The source at main.go:26 is attacker-controlled and the trace lines are accurate, but the exact hostname membership check at main.go:27 is a closing guard under the stated criteria, so the candidate is refuted. The redirect gap is real: the allowlist covers only the initial URL and `http.Get` at main.go:31 follows redirects with no CheckRedirect, so an allowed host that redirects internally would bypass it. That exploit depends on redirect behavior the code does not show, so if redirect bypass is the concern, it should be tracked as a separate finding rather than as this one.
